title: How To Give A Warning That Improves Behavior https://smartclassroommanagement.com/2010/05/22/how-to-give-a-warning-that-improves-behavior/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Continuing from an earlier article on making warnings a first consequence, Linsin explains exactly how to deliver one so it has maximum impact. A warning, he argues, should be nothing more than a warning: no lecture, scolding, or added commentary, since its purpose is to let students correct their own behavior and demonstrate that the teacher trusts them to do so. He describes two variations: silently marking the warning (a name on the board, a flipped card) when the student clearly knows which rule was broken, used about 75% of the time; and a brief, matter-of-fact spoken statement of the broken rule for the remaining cases. He stresses applying warnings consistently to every student, including top performers, and backing warnings with a consequence students genuinely dislike. Linsin frames this 'hit and run' approach as an enduring strategy that grows more effective the more consistently it's used, since it firmly places responsibility for behavior on the student.
points: A warning should be given quickly, dispassionately, and without any lecture, scolding, or added commentary.
Use a silent method (name on the board, flipped card) about 75% of the time when students clearly know which rule they broke.
For the remaining cases, deliver a brief, matter-of-fact spoken statement of the rule broken, then immediately walk away.
Apply warnings consistently to every student, including top performers, to demonstrate teacher integrity and consistency.
Warnings only work when backed by a real consequence students dislike for the next infraction.
quotes: A warning is just a warning—and nothing more. So when you give one to a student for breaking a rule, leave it at that.
A warning only works when its purpose is to allow students to fix their mistakes on their own.
You have to give trust before students will show you they’re worthy of it.

If a student breaks a rule, and you’re sure the student knows what rule was broken, then you simply write his or her name on the board, place a yellow card in the student’s designated pocket, or do whatever you do to signify a warning.
Even the most well-behaved students make mistakes once in a while. Resist the urge to look the other way when they break a rule.
When your students begin to grasp that the responsibility for breaking rules in your classroom falls firmly—and solely—in their laps, behavior will improve.
